paras: The expulsion of Dr. Howard from Hattiesburg was an order, reported in late August 1905, that a Black physician leave Hattiesburg, Mississippi. The only known account, a brief editorial note in the Oklahoma Safeguard, does not say who gave the order or whether he left. The paper treated the case as an example of the "move-on" orders it said were given to Black men who prospered in the South.

In its issue of August 31, 1905, the Safeguard said it had learned "a few days ago" that "Dr. Howard has been notified to leave Hattiesburg." No first name, age or details of his practice appear in the note. According to the paper, he had not offended anyone, and the order stemmed from "his color and success in his profession," though the printed text of that passage is partly garbled. The note names no one who delivered the order and reports no violence against him.

The coverage does not show whether Dr. Howard left Hattiesburg, and no arrest, investigation or official response is reported. The Safeguard instead called on the Mississippi legislature to "take steps on this practice" and to pass laws preventing "a set of men" from committing such "outrages" on others, "be they white or black."

The story appeared under the headline "Negro Doctor Ordered to Leave" on the front page of the Oklahoma Safeguard, a Black weekly. Its editorial generalized from the case, arguing that when a Black man's success was "antagonistic to his white brother" in the same trade, "they simply order him away." Such orders, the paper wrote, left the recipient to "move or die," or saw his business destroyed with "nobody" held responsible.

The Safeguard called the practice "a shame" and "an outrage" and asked how the government could protect Cuba "from the Spanish oppression" yet not "the humblest of its own citizens." No report of the order was found in the white press or in other Black papers, and the Safeguard printed no follow-up.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The Oklahoma Safeguard reported that Dr. Howard had been notified to leave Hattiesburg though he had offended no one, tying the order to his color and success, and described "move-on" orders as a Southern practice enforced by threat of death or ruin.

framing.detail: Under "Negro Doctor Ordered to Leave," the Safeguard called the practice "a shame" and "an outrage," asked how the government could protect Cuba but not "the humblest of its own citizens," and urged legislation.

record_check.dossier: The article names no county; only the town (Hattiesburg) and state are given.

record_check.record: Whites ordered Dr. Howard ... to leave town
record_check.dossier: The article says he "has been notified to leave" without naming who notified him; whiteness of those responsible is implied by the editorial's general discussion of white competitors, not stated for this case.
Supported as late August 1905 (learned "a few days ago" before August 31); no exact date.
No justification from those who gave the notice is reported; the paper attributes it to his color and professional success.

sources.note: "Negro Doctor Ordered to Leave": Dr. Howard notified to leave Hattiesburg; editorial on "move-on" orders; only report found; OCR partly garbled.
quotes: Dr. Howard has been notified to leave Hattiesburg
He has not offended any one and the one who offended him has his color and success in his profession.
They give the Negro the "move-on" orders.
When these orders are given you, you will have to move or die; or your business is destroyed and nobody is held responsible for your life or property.
The legislature should take steps on this practice in Mississippi
